    anomalies

    An anomaly tracker: one thin lane per metric over time, the band it was expected to stay in as a faint fill, the expected value as a hairline, the actual as a line, and every day it stepped outside the band as a flagged dot.

    Patterns across two dimensions or a cycle Trend over time Exact values and lookup

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Watching a dozen daily measures at once and seeing which stepped out of line: net new money, fees, trades, complaints
    • Operations and risk monitoring, where the exceptions matter more than the levels

    Least useful for

    • Comparing the levels of the measures with each other (each lane has its own scale; use line)
    • One measure only (use line with a band)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per combination of two categories, such as month and product. How it is built: One lane per metric over the shared time axis, each on its own scale: the expected band as a faint fill, the expected value as a hairline, the actual as a line, flagged readings as alert dots; lanes sorted by how many were flagged. Reads well with 14 to 3000 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    xdateyesField with the date or period of each reading.
    metriccategoryyesField naming the measure each row belongs to; each measure is one lane.
    valuenumberyesField with the reading.
    expectednumberField with the value expected that day, drawn as a hairline through the band.
    lownumberField with the bottom of the expected band. Needs high too.
    highnumberField with the top of the expected band. Needs low too.
    flagcategoryField that is true on anomalous readings (true, 1, "yes"). Flagged readings draw as filled dots in the alert color. Without it, readings outside the band are flagged.

    Not possible with this data (26)
    • board: It needs a stage or status column with a handful of values, and a name per row.
    • bullet: It needs a target, plan or budget column.
    • candlestick: It needs open, high, low and close prices per period.
    • chord: It needs flows that go both ways between the same groups.
    • choropleth: needs a column of country or state codes that sit on a basemap
    • dual: It needs two measures over the same periods, in two columns.
    • dumbbell: It needs the same measure at two points in time, in two columns.
    • funnel: It needs ordered stages that narrow, such as visits to sign-ups to sales.
    • history: It needs dated events with a short title each.
    • lifecycle: view: stages needs at least two date fields in order, such as ["proposed", "adopted"].
    • likert: It needs answer counts on one ordered scale, such as disagree to agree.
    • locator: needs named places with region codes on a basemap, or coordinates
    • matrix: It needs one row per pair of two categories, such as topic and quarter.
    • meter: It needs a target, plan or budget column.
    • pyramid: It needs two counts per ordered band, such as women and men per age group.
    • ragboard: It needs status columns holding R, A, G (or red, amber, green), one row per client or deal; the rag transform makes them from numbers.
    • ragtrend: It needs one status (R, A, G) per entity per period.
    • rings: It needs a target, plan or budget column.
    • slope: It needs the same measure at two points in time, in two columns.
    • strips: It needs whole counts per row, in one or more part columns.
    • symbols: needs a column of country or state codes that sit on a basemap, or coordinates
    • timeline: It needs tasks with a start date.
    • variance: It needs a target, plan or budget column.
    • waterfall: It needs changes that add up from one total to another.
    • whitespace: It needs one row per client and product with a state: held, an opportunity, or not eligible.
    • xray: It needs one row: one client with its facts, holdings and share of wallet.

    area

    A line with a soft filled area down to zero, for a trend where the amount itself matters.

    Trend over time How each group or period splits Comparing amounts across categories

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Volumes over time where the amount itself matters: cash, revenue, traffic
    • A forecast with its uncertainty band
    • How a stacked total splits over time (two to four series)

    Least useful for

    • Several series that cross: the fills hide each other (use line)
    • Categories with no order (use bar)
    • Values that go below zero

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per point in time, in order. How it is built: One point per row at x (in date order) and y; the area under the line is filled down to zero. Several y fields stack or overlap; a forecast field continues the line dashed, and a band (low, high) shades a range. Reads well with 4 to 400 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    xdateyesField for the ordered axis, usually a date or period.
    ynumber (one or more)yesField or fields for the values. Each field is one series.
    forecastcategoryField that is true on forecast rows. From the last actual on, lines draw dashed in a softly shaded zone labelled Forecast, and the tooltip marks those rows. On an area the forecast's wash is fainter too. Unstacked areas only.

    bar

    Vertical bars comparing amounts across categories.

    Comparing amounts across categories Ranking, top to bottom Trend over time How each group or period splits Share of one whole Actual against target or plan Exact values and lookup

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • An amount across a handful of categories: revenue by region, orders by month
    • Two or three series side by side or stacked: Core and Plus by region
    • Monthly totals against a budget line

    Least useful for

    • Long category names (use hbar)
    • More than about 15 categories (use hbar or treemap)
    • A long continuous trend (use line)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One bar per row at x, as tall as y. Several y fields make grouped bars, or stacked ones with stacked (percent for shares); a lines field draws a line such as a target across the bars. Reads well with 2 to 16 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    xcategoryyesField for the categories along the horizontal axis.
    ynumber (one or more)yesField or fields for bar heights. Each field is one series.
    linesnumber (one or more)Field or fields drawn as lines over the bars, on the same axis, for example a target. Never a second axis. Under one target line (a field named target, plan, goal, budget or quota), bars on the wrong side of it (see goodWhen) are drawn outlined and keyed Below target.
    comparenumberField drawn as a wider, quieter column behind each bar, on the same axis, for a comparison such as last year or the plan. The key names it by its label and the tooltip gives its value. One y series, unstacked.

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Every individual deal, order or response visible, with outliers you can name
    • Spread across a few groups in samples of tens to hundreds

    Least useful for

    One row is: One row per thing measured (a deal, a ticket, a response); the chart counts or spreads them. How it is built: One dot per row along the value axis, nudged apart so none overlap; a group field gives each group its own row, and a label field names each dot on hover. Reads well with 10 to 400 rows.

    groupcategoryField giving each group its own labelled row.

    board

    A status board: one column per stage with its count in the header, and the items in it as quiet cards, so where everything stands reads at a glance.

    Exact values and lookup Conversion through ordered steps Comparing amounts across categories Schedules and plans

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Where everything stands in a lifecycle: regulations by status, deals by stage, tickets by state
    • Seeing at once which stage is crowded and what is in it, by name

    Least useful for

    • Amounts per stage alone (use funnel or bar)
    • Hundreds of items (filter first, or count them into a funnel)
    • Stages with no natural order

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One column per stage (in the order of stages, or of first appearance) headed by its count, and one card per row in its stage's column, with a group dot, a value and a detail line when those fields are given. Reads well with 3 to 120 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each card.
    stagecategoryyesField with each item's stage: one column per distinct value, in the order of stages or of first appearance.
    groupcategoryField that colors a dot on each card by group, with a key. Up to 8 groups stay distinct.
    valuenumberField written on each card, such as impact or amount, in the field's format.
    detailcategoryField for a smaller line under the card's name, such as the issuer or the owner.

    boxplot

    A box plot per group on one shared axis: a box over the middle half of the values (first to third quartile), a line at the median, whiskers to the furthest values within 1.5 box-widths, and dots for outliers beyond.

    How values spread Comparing amounts across categories

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Comparing medians and spread across groups: deal size by region, handle time by team
    • Spotting outliers in analytic reviews

    Least useful for

    • Audiences who do not read quartiles (use beeswarm or ridgeline)
    • Fewer than about five values per group
    • Totals

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per thing measured (a deal, a ticket, a response); the chart counts or spreads them. How it is built: Rows are grouped by group; each group's values give a box from the first to the third quartile, a line at the median, whiskers and outlier dots. Reads well with 15 to any number of rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    valuenumberyesNumeric field whose spread is drawn.
    groupcategoryField giving each group its own box. Without it, all rows make one box.

    bump

    Rank over time: in every period the series are ranked by value (highest first), and each series is one smooth line through its ranks, named at both ends.

    Ranking, top to bottom Trend over time

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • How a ranking changes over time: products, teams, channels by month
    • Who overtook whom

    Least useful for

    • When the size of the gaps matters, as ranks hide it (use line)
    • More than about ten series, or only one period

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per combination of two categories, such as month and product. How it is built: Rows are one per period and series; in each period the series are ranked by value and each series is a line through its ranks. Reads well with 6 to any number of rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    xdateyesField with the period, such as a month. Periods keep the order of the rows.
    seriescategoryyesField naming the series being ranked, such as a product.
    valuenumberyesField the ranking is by; the highest value ranks 1.

    candlestick

    Prices per period as candles: a thin wick from low to high around a body from open to close, in the up color when the period closed higher and the down color when lower.

    Trend over time How values spread Exact values and lookup

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Prices per period: share price, exchange rates, commodity prices
    • Volatility and the open-to-close move in trading reports

    Least useful for

    • Anything without open, high, low and close (use line)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per point in time, in order. How it is built: One candle per row: a wick from low to high and a body from open to close, colored up or down; an optional moving average line. Reads well with 5 to 250 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    xdateyesField with the period, such as a trading day.
    opennumberyesField with the opening price.
    highnumberyesField with the highest price.
    lownumberyesField with the lowest price.
    closenumberyesField with the closing price.

    chord

    Flows between groups around a circle: each group an arc as long as everything it sends and receives, each flow a ribbon from its sender to its receiver, in the sender's color.

    Flows between stages or groups How two measures relate

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Two-way flows among the same groups: customers moving between plans, trade between regions

    Least useful for

    • One-way chains of stages (use sankey)
    • Reading exact amounts (use table)
    • More than about ten groups

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per flow, from a source to a target. How it is built: Each group is an arc as long as everything it sends and receives; each row is a ribbon from source to target, as thick as value. Reads well with 3 to 60 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    sourcecategoryyesField naming where each flow comes from.
    targetcategoryyesField naming where each flow goes.
    valuenumberyesField with each flow's size.

    choropleth

    A map with each region shaded by its value, from the weakest tint to the strongest, with a scale under it: revenue by country, share by state.

    Comparing amounts across categories Patterns across two dimensions or a cycle Exact values and lookup

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • An amount or a rate by country or state: revenue by country, share by state
    • Seeing where something is high or low across a territory

    Least useful for

    • Exact comparisons between regions (use hbar)
    • Totals that follow area or population, which big regions exaggerate (use a rate, or symbols)
    • Rows that are not regions

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One region per row, matched by its code to the basemap (a built-in tile grid or your GeoJSON), shaded on a seven-step scale from the lowest value to the highest; regions with no row stay grey. Reads well with 3 to 300 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    idcategoryyesField with each row's region code: a country or state code on a built-in basemap (FR, TX), or the feature id in your GeoJSON.
    valuenumberField that shades each region on the sequential scale. Rows with no number stay grey. Give value or category, not both.
    categorycategoryField that colors each region by its category instead, one series color per value with a key: a transposition status, a supervisor, a regime. Up to 8 categories stay distinct.
    previousnumberField with the same measure in the previous period, such as last year's revenue. Each region's tooltip then gives the change, and show "change" shades by it.

    donut

    Part-to-whole at a glance: a ring of up to 6 slices with the total in the middle and a legend of values and shares.

    Share of one whole A headline number Comparing amounts across categories

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Share of one whole with two to five parts: revenue by segment, budget by team
    • An executive summary where the total matters too

    Least useful for

    • More than six parts or close values (use hbar)
    • Comparing several wholes (use bar stacked to percent)
    • Change over time (use area)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One slice per row, its angle its share of the sum of value, with the total in the middle. Reads well with 2 to 6 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each slice.
    valuenumberyesField with each slice's amount. Zero, negative and missing values are left out.

    dot

    A dot plot: one row per item and one dot per measure on one shared axis, with a hairline across each row.

    Comparing amounts across categories Ranking, top to bottom Exact values and lookup Change between two points

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Two to five measures of one kind per item: ease, value and support scores by product
    • Rankings where the differences matter more than the amounts: prices, rates, scores
    • Many rows with far less ink than bars

    Least useful for

    • Amounts where the length from zero matters (use hbar)
    • Measures on different scales (use table or radar)
    • Exactly a before and an after (use dumbbell)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One row per data row with a hairline across and one dot per values field at its value on one shared axis; one field writes its value beside the dot, several take series colors. Reads well with 2 to 30 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each row.
    valuenumber (one or more)yesField or fields placed as dots on the axis. Each field is one series with its own color; one field writes its value beside the dot. Also accepts `values`, the older name.

    dual

    Two measures with different units, such as revenue and churn, one above the other on two panels that share one time axis, each on its own scale.

    Trend over time How two measures relate Comparing amounts across categories

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Two measures in different units over the same periods: revenue and churn, visits and conversion rate
    • Showing whether two shapes move together without a misleading second axis

    Least useful for

    • Two series in the same unit (use line, one axis)
    • More than two measures (use horizon or small multiples)
    • Categories with no order (use bar)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per point in time, in order. How it is built: Two panels one above the other sharing the x axis: y on the top panel and y2 on the bottom, each on its own scale, drawn as bars (from zero) or lines. Reads well with 3 to 200 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    xdateyesField for the shared axis, usually a date or period.
    ynumberyesMeasure on the top panel.
    y2numberyesMeasure on the bottom panel, in its own unit.

    Before and after per item on one shared axis: a muted dot for before, an accent dot for after, joined by a line (a range plot).

    gauge

    One headline number on a half-circle scale: an arc filled from min to the value, a tick at the target, the number large inside the arc and the scale's ends below; with a target, a line under the arc says where it stands (Target met, or how far to go).

    A headline number Actual against target or plan

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • One KPI against a goal on a known scale: NPS, utilization, SLA attainment

    Least useful for

    • Several values (use bullet or meter)
    • Trends (use kpi with series)
    • Small differences, which the arc hides

    The table it needs

    One row is: One value; with more rows, the last one is the headline and the rest draw its trend. How it is built: The first row's value fills a half-circle from min to max, with a tick at target and the number in the middle. Reads well with 1 to 1 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    valuenumberyesField holding the number.
    targetnumberField holding the target, marked with a tick.

    hbar

    Horizontal bars for rankings and long labels: label on the left, bar, value at the end.

    Ranking, top to bottom Comparing amounts across categories Exact values and lookup Actual against target or plan

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Rankings with long names: top features, top customers, causes
    • Up to about 30 categories, readable on a phone
    • Two or three measures per row, side by side, stacked, or split into columns when their units differ

    Least useful for

    • Time order (use bar or line)
    • Share of one whole (use donut or waffle)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One horizontal bar per row, label on the left and value at the end, sorted as given or by value. Several value fields draw one thin bar each per row, stacked into one bar with stacked (percent for shares), or in one column per field with split. Reads well with 2 to 30 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each bar.
    valuenumber (one or more)yesField or fields with each bar's amount. Bars start at zero. Several fields draw one bar per field in each row (grouped), stacked into one bar with stacked, or in separate columns with split.

    ycategoryyesField for the rows.

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    One row is: One row per thing measured (a deal, a ticket, a response); the chart counts or spreads them. How it is built: The range of value is cut into bins on round edges; each bar counts the rows in its bin. Reads well with 20 to any number of rows.

    valuenumberyesNumeric field to bin.

    history

    A client's story as a vertical timeline: one event per row with its date, title, an optional second line and an amount, newest first, a dot per event colored by kind with a key, and the month written wherever it changes.

    Schedules and plans Exact values and lookup Trend over time

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • A client's story: meetings, calls, trades, campaigns and complaints in one scroll
    • What happened before a churn, a complaint or a big trade
    • Several clients' recent activity side by side

    Least useful for

    • Amounts over time, where the shape matters (use line)
    • Tasks with a start and an end (use timeline)
    • Counting events per period (use bar or calendar)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per thing measured (a deal, a ticket, a response); the chart counts or spreads them. How it is built: One event per row sorted by date, newest first, each a dot colored by kind on a vertical rail with its date, title, note and amount; the month is written where it changes, and a group field makes one rail per value. Reads well with 3 to 400 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    datedateyesField with when the event happened.
    titlecategoryyesField with the event in a few words.
    kindcategoryField with the kind of event (Meeting, Call, Trade); each kind takes a color and a letter, keyed.
    notecategoryField with a second, smaller line under the title.
    amountnumberField with an amount to write at the right of the event, where there is one.
    groupcategoryField that splits the events into one list per value (one per client), each under its own heading.

    horizon

    Many time series at once, each in a thin row: values are measured from a baseline and folded into bands of deepening color, blue above and red below, so a dozen series fit where one line chart would.

    Trend over time Comparing amounts across categories Actual against target or plan

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Many series over time in little space: six to twenty regions, servers or stores
    • Deviation from plan, day by day, in operations monitoring

    Least useful for

    • General audiences and exact values (use line)
    • One or two series

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per point in time, in order. How it is built: One thin row per y field; each value is measured from a baseline and folded into bands of deepening color, blue above and red below. Reads well with 10 to any number of rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    xdateyesField for the ordered axis, usually a date.
    ynumber (one or more)yesField or fields, one row each, such as a region's revenue against plan.

    icicle

    A hierarchy laid flat: a column for the total, then one per level left to right, each child splitting its parent's height by value, in lighter tints of its family's color.

    Nested breakdowns Share of one whole Ranking, top to bottom

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Deep breakdowns with long names: budget by unit, team and line
    • Drill paths, left to right

    Least useful for

    • Flat data with one level (use hbar)
    • Negative values

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per leaf of the hierarchy, its levels in columns from the top down. How it is built: A column for the total, then one per level; each child splits its parent's height by the sum of value. Reads well with 4 to 200 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    levelscategory (one or more)yesFields from the top level down, one column each, for example ["region", "product", "plan"]. Up to 4.
    valuenumberyesField sizing the cells. Zero and negative values are left out.

    • dumbbell: needs a separate column for to (it would reuse "revenue", already the from)

    • locator: needs named places with region codes on a basemap, or coordinates
    • matrix: It needs one row per pair of two categories, such as topic and quarter.

    • pyramid: needs a separate column for right (it would reuse "revenue", already the left)

    • slope: needs a separate column for to (it would reuse "revenue", already the from)

    • symbols: needs a column of country or state codes that sit on a basemap, or coordinates
    • timeline: needs a date column for start
    • variance: needs a separate column for target (it would reuse "revenue", already the value)
    • waterfall: It needs changes that add up from one total to another.
    • whitespace: It needs one row per client and product with a state: held, an opportunity, or not eligible.
    • xray: It needs one row: one client with its facts, holdings and share of wallet.

    lifecycle

    Stage swimlanes: one row per item on a shared date axis, each stage drawn from its date to the next in a deepening tint of one hue, a tick at every stage date, and the last reached stage running on faintly while its next date is unknown.

    Schedules and plans Change between two points Exact values and lookup

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Where each regulation stands: proposed, adopted, in force, applies
    • What applies next, and how long since adoption
    • Any multi-stage process with dates per stage: deals, hiring, product launches

    Least useful for

    • One start and one end per row (use timeline)
    • Stages with no dates (use funnel or table)
    • More than about 30 rows (filter, or facet by group)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One row per data row on a shared date axis: from each stage's date to the next a segment in a deepening tint, a tick at every date, a faint run from the last known stage to the edge when the next date is missing, a today line, and a status pill at the end; impact sets the row's thickness. Reads well with 1 to 30 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each row.
    stagesdate (one or more)yesDate fields in lifecycle order, such as proposed, adopted, inForce, applies. A later date may be missing: the row then runs on from its last known stage.
    groupcategoryField that gathers rows under a heading, such as topic.
    statuscategoryField written as a small pill at the row's end, such as In force or Consultation.
    impactnumberField from 1 to 5 that sets each row's thickness: the higher the impact, the thicker the row.

    likert

    Survey answers as diverging stacked bars: one bar per question, its responses in order from one pole to the other, centered on the neutral middle so disagreement grows left and agreement right.

    Survey and rating answers Share of one whole Comparing amounts across categories

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Agree and disagree scales: employee and customer surveys
    • Comparing sentiment across questions

    Least useful for

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One bar per row (a question); its response fields, in order from one pole to the other, stack centered on the neutral middle. Reads well with 1 to 20 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField with each question.
    valuenumber (one or more)yesCount fields for the responses, in order from the negative pole to the positive, for example ["strongly_disagree", "disagree", "neutral", "agree", "strongly_agree"]. An odd count puts the middle one at the center. Also accepts `responses`, the older name.

    line

    Lines showing change over an ordered axis, usually time.

    Trend over time Comparing amounts across categories Actual against target or plan

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Change over time: revenue, users, cost by month
    • Several series compared over time
    • Progress against a target or a forecast

    Least useful for

    • Categories with no order (use bar)
    • Share of a whole (use donut or area stacked)
    • Only two points in time (use slope)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per point in time, in order. How it is built: One point per row at x (in order) and y, joined; each y field is one series, and reference lines mark targets. Reads well with 3 to 1000 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    xdateyesField for the ordered axis, usually a date or period.
    ynumber (one or more)yesField or fields for line values. Each field is one series.
    forecastcategoryField that is true on forecast rows. From the last actual on, lines draw dashed in a softly shaded zone labelled Forecast, and the tooltip marks those rows.

    locator

    A small, clean map that says where things are: a marker and an always-on name for each place, such as offices, stores or sites, with a second line of detail if there is one.

    Exact values and lookup

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Where the offices, stores or sites are, by name
    • A handful of named places for a report or a page header

    Least useful for

    • Amounts per place (use symbols)
    • More than about 30 places, where names collide (use symbols or a table)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One marker per row on its region (by code) or at its coordinates, its name written beside it; a kind field colors the markers with a key. Reads well with 1 to 30 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField with each place's name, written beside its marker.
    idcategoryField with the region code that places each marker: a country or state code on a built-in basemap, or the feature id in your GeoJSON. Use lat and lon instead for coordinates.
    latnumberField with each row's latitude, for placing by coordinates on your own GeoJSON (not on a built-in grid).
    lonnumberField with each row's longitude, paired with lat.
    notecategoryField with a second, smaller line under the name, such as a city or a headcount.
    colorcategoryField that colors the markers by kind, with a key. Also accepts `kind`, the older name.

    marimekko

    A mosaic: one column per category, as wide as its total, split into segments by each series' share of that column.

    How each group or period splits Share of one whole Comparing amounts across categories

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Market maps: how big each segment is and how it splits (region by product)
    • Sizing opportunities in strategy reviews

    Least useful for

    • Many small segments
    • Precise values (use table)
    • Audiences new to mosaics (use bar stacked)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per combination of two categories, such as month and product. How it is built: One column per x category, as wide as its total; each column is split by series into segments as tall as their share. Reads well with 4 to 60 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    xcategoryyesField naming each column, such as a region. Columns keep the order of the rows.
    seriescategoryyesField naming the segments inside each column, such as a product.
    valuenumberyesNumeric field sizing the segments; a column's width is the sum of its values.

    matrix

    A mark matrix (a punchcard): one mark per pair of x and y, sized by a value, shaded by another, or a square where a flag is yes.

    Patterns across two dimensions or a cycle Comparing amounts across categories Exact values and lookup

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Regulatory pressure per topic per quarter: how many new obligations, how hard they bite
    • Who must comply with which rule: one square per yes
    • Any two categories crossed, where a heatmap's shade alone says too little

    Least useful for

    • One category only (use hbar or dot)
    • Exact values to read off (use table with heat cells)
    • More than about 24 columns or 30 rows

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per combination of two categories, such as month and product. How it is built: One mark per row at its x column and y row: a circle sized by size, shaded by color (a number on the seven-step scale, a category by its color), or a square where mark is yes; pairs with no row stay empty. Reads well with 4 to 400 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    xcategoryyesField for the columns: quarters, stakeholders, stages.
    ycategoryyesField for the rows: topics, regulations, teams.
    sizenumberField that sizes each circle, by area, against the largest value.
    colorcategoryField that shades each mark: a number takes the seven-step scale from lowest to highest (with a scale under the grid), a category takes one color per value (with a key).
    flagcategoryA yes/no field (true, 1, "yes", "x"): a filled square where it is yes, an empty cell where it is no. For who must comply. Also accepts `mark`, the older name.
    labelcategoryField (text or a number) written inside marks big enough to hold it; always in the tooltip.

    mustComply Must complybooleanflag2 different: true, false

    pareto

    The 80/20 view: categories sorted largest first as bars of their share of the total, a line through the running total, and a dashed line at the threshold.

    What drives or moves a total Ranking, top to bottom Share of one whole

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • The few causes behind most of a total: ticket causes, defects, returns, costs
    • Deciding where to act first

    Least useful for

    • Time order (use bar)
    • Fewer than four categories
    • Negative values

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: Rows sorted largest first as bars of their share of the total, a line through the running total and a dashed line at the threshold (80% by default). Reads well with 4 to 25 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each category.
    valuenumberyesField with each category's count or amount. Zero and negative values are left out.

    pie

    Part-to-whole as a full disc: up to 6 slices from twelve o'clock clockwise, each wide in proportion to its share, with the shares written on the slices and a legend of values.

    Share of one whole Comparing amounts across categories

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Share of one whole with two to five parts, where the shares themselves are the point: votes, market share
    • Small multiples of one split per group (facet), the same part in the same color everywhere

    Least useful for

    • More than six parts or close values (use hbar)
    • When the total matters too (use donut)
    • Change over time (use area)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One wedge per row from twelve o'clock clockwise, its angle its share of the sum of value, the share written on it. Reads well with 2 to 6 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each slice.
    valuenumberyesField with each slice's amount. Zero, negative and missing values are left out.

    pyramid

    A population pyramid: one row per band (an age group, a tenure band), with two counts as bars growing out from a center axis on one shared scale, the left count leftward and the right count rightward.

    How values spread Comparing amounts across categories How each group or period splits

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Two groups across ordered bands: women and men by age group, new and returning customers by tenure

    Least useful for

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One row per band in the order given; the left field's count grows leftward from a center axis and the right field's rightward, both on one shared scale. Reads well with 3 to 30 rows.

    labelcategoryyesField naming each band, in order from top to bottom, such as the age group.
    leftnumberyesField with the count drawn leftward, such as women.
    rightnumberyesField with the count drawn rightward, such as men.

    ragboard

    A RAG scorecard: one row per entity (a client, a relationship manager, a deal) and one Red, Amber or Green cell per dimension, worst first, with an overall column holding each row's worst status.

    Actual against target or plan Exact values and lookup Comparing amounts across categories

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • A RAG scorecard: client health, coverage, pipeline and relationship status per client or per relationship manager
    • Which accounts need action first, and on what
    • Status reviews where each cell is a judgment, not an amount

    Least useful for

    • Amounts and trends (use table with heat cells, or line)
    • One status over many periods (use ragtrend)
    • More than about 40 rows (filter to the ones that need attention)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One row per data row and one cell per dimension holding its status (R, A, G or N) as a shape, an Overall column with the worst of them first, rows sorted worst first, a strip that counts the statuses above and a count per column below; a previous field per dimension adds a better or worse arrow. Reads well with 2 to 40 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each row: the client, the relationship manager or the deal.
    dimensionscategory (one or more)yesStatus fields, one column each, holding R, A, G or N (or red, amber, green, grey). The rag transform turns numbers into them.
    groupcategoryField that gathers rows under headings, such as segment or perspective.
    notecategoryField written small under each name, such as the action owner or the next step.

    ragtrend

    RAG status over time: one row per entity and one small mark per period, shaped and colored by its status (a filled circle On track, a triangle At risk, a square Off track).

    Change between two points Trend over time Actual against target or plan

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • How each client's or deal's status moved, review by review
    • Spotting who slipped recently, and reading why
    • Monthly or quarterly RAG reporting with a history

    Least useful for

    • Several dimensions at one moment (use ragboard)
    • Numbers rather than statuses (use line or horizon)
    • More than about 24 periods (roll them up)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per combination of two categories, such as month and product. How it is built: One row per entity and one cell per period with its status as a shape, a tick where the status changed, the note of why in the tooltip, and the current status as a pill at the end; rows worst-current first. Reads well with 6 to 600 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each row: the client, the relationship manager or the deal.
    perioddateyesField with each row's period: a month, a quarter or a review date, in order.
    statuscategoryyesField with the status in that period: R, A, G or N (or red, amber, green, grey).
    notecategoryField saying why the status moved, shown in the tooltip of the period where it changed.

    ridgeline

    One smooth distribution curve per group on a shared axis, overlapping like a mountain range: how values spread in each group, for example deal sizes by region.

    How values spread Comparing amounts across categories Trend over time

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Comparing distribution shapes across many groups: deal size by region, latency by month

    Least useful for

    • Few values per group (use beeswarm)
    • Exact statistics (use boxplot)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per thing measured (a deal, a ticket, a response); the chart counts or spreads them. How it is built: Rows are grouped by group; each group's values become a smooth density curve, the curves overlapping on one axis. Reads well with 20 to any number of rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    valuenumberyesNumeric field whose distribution is drawn.
    groupcategoryyesField giving each group its own ridge.

    rings

    Concentric progress rings, one per row from the outside in, each filled to its share of target; past the target a second lap shows how far over.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each goal.
    valuenumberyesField with the amount reached.
    targetnumberyesField with the goal amount.

    rose

    A polar area chart (a Nightingale rose) for a cycle that wraps round, such as hours of the day or months of the year: one equal wedge per row, clockwise from twelve o'clock, its area true to its value.

    Patterns across two dimensions or a cycle Comparing amounts across categories

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Cycles that wrap round: hours of the day, months of the year, directions

    Least useful for

    • Categories with no cycle (use bar)
    • Precise comparisons

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One equal wedge per row, clockwise from twelve o'clock, its area true to value; several y fields stack. Reads well with 4 to 36 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each wedge, in cycle order, such as the hour or the month.
    ynumber (one or more)yesField or fields with the values; each field is one ring of the stack. Up to 4 stay readable.

    sankey

    Flows between stages as ribbons as thick as their volume, for example traffic source to landing page to outcome.

    Flows between stages or groups Nested breakdowns What drives or moves a total

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Flows through stages: traffic source to page to outcome, budget to spend
    • Where volume goes and where it is lost

    Least useful for

    One row is: One row per flow, from a source to a target. How it is built: Each row is a ribbon from source to target, as thick as value; nodes stack into stages left to right. Reads well with 2 to 80 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    sourcecategoryyesField naming where each flow starts.
    targetcategoryyesField naming where each flow ends.
    valuenumberyesField with each flow's volume.

    scatter

    One dot per row placed by two numbers, to show how they relate.

    How two measures relate How values spread Exact values and lookup

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Whether two measures move together: growth and margin, price and volume
    • Segments and quadrants, and the accounts that stand out

    Least useful for

    • One measure only (use histogram)
    • Trends over time (use line)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per thing measured (a deal, a ticket, a response); the chart counts or spreads them. How it is built: One dot per row at x and y (both numbers); size and series add a third and fourth field, and label names each dot. Reads well with 6 to 2000 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    xnumberyesNumeric field along the horizontal axis.
    ynumberyesNumeric field along the vertical axis.
    sizenumberField sizing each dot by area, making a bubble chart: four times the value, twice the radius. Bigger bubbles are drawn first.
    colorcategoryField that groups the dots by color. Up to 3 groups stay distinct. Also accepts `series`, the older name.
    labelcategoryField naming each dot in its tooltip.
    clustercategoryField naming each dot's cluster, such as a segment found by analysis. A soft, rounded hull gathers each cluster's dots and carries its name at the middle, so the areas read as regions of the plot; the dots take the cluster's color unless color is set. Up to 6 clusters.

    slope

    Each item's move between two points in time, as a line from a left column to a right one on one shared scale.

    Change between two points Ranking, top to bottom

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Two points in time: H1 against H2, last year against this
    • Seeing who rose, who fell and who swapped places

    Least useful for

    • More than two periods (use line or bump)
    • More than about 15 items, where lines tangle (use dumbbell)

    strips

    Unit strips: one row per item with a strip of small squares, one per unit, colored part by part in order (mandatory, recommended, optional), the total and the first part's share at the end.

    How each group or period splits Comparing amounts across categories Share of one whole

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • How many provisions each regulation has and how many are binding (mandatory, recommended, optional)
    • Density: provisions per page, when per is set
    • Counts people can see as things, not lengths

    Least useful for

    • Amounts that are not counts, such as money (use hbar stacked)
    • More than about 20 rows (use hbar stacked)
    • Shares of one whole across items (use waffle or donut)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One row per data row with one small square per unit, filled part by part in order (each part its color), the total and the first part's share written at the end; when totals run long, one square stands for a round number of units. Reads well with 1 to 20 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each row.
    valuenumber (one or more)yesField or fields with each part's count, in the order they are drawn. The first part's share of the total is written at the end. Also accepts `parts`, the older name.
    pernumberField with a denominator, such as pages: the density (units per one of them) is written at the end and in the tooltip.

    sunburst

    A hierarchy as rings: the inner ring splits the total by the first level, each outer ring splits its parent's slice by the next level, in lighter tints of the parent's color.

    Nested breakdowns Share of one whole

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Two or three level part-to-whole: revenue by product, then region
    • An overview that invites a closer look

    Least useful for

    • Precise comparisons (use icicle or hbar)
    • Deep levels with long names (use icicle)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per leaf of the hierarchy, its levels in columns from the top down. How it is built: The inner ring splits the total by the first level; each outer ring splits its parent by the next level, by the sum of value. Reads well with 4 to 120 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    levelscategory (one or more)yesFields from the top level down, one ring each, for example ["product", "region"]. Up to 3.
    valuenumberyesField sizing the slices. Zero and negative values are left out.

    symbols

    A map with a circle on each place, its area true to a value: customers by state, volume by port.

    Comparing amounts across categories Patterns across two dimensions or a cycle

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Counts and totals by place where the size itself matters: customers by state, volume by port
    • Several kinds of place on one map, told apart by color

    Least useful for

    • Rates and shares (use choropleth)
    • Hundreds of overlapping places (sum them by region first)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One circle per row on its region (by code) or at its coordinates, its area true to the size field; a color field groups the circles with a key. Reads well with 2 to 150 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    sizenumberyesField that sizes each circle, by area. Zero and missing values draw nothing.
    idcategoryField with the region code that places each circle: a country or state code on a built-in basemap, or the feature id in your GeoJSON. Use lat and lon instead for coordinates.
    latnumberField with each row's latitude, for placing by coordinates on your own GeoJSON (not on a built-in grid).
    lonnumberField with each row's longitude, paired with lat.
    labelcategoryField naming each place in its tooltip. Defaults to the region's name, or the id.
    colorcategoryField that colors the circles by group, with a key.

    timeline

    A Gantt-style timeline: one row per task with a bar from its start to its end date, a diamond for milestones (no end), month ticks along the top and an optional today line.

    Schedules and plans

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Project plans, launch phases and milestones
    • What is late or running now

    Least useful for

    • Quantities (use bar)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One row per task with a bar from start to end, a diamond where there is no end (a milestone), grouped and with a today line. Reads well with 1 to 40 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each task.
    startdateyesField with each task's start date, as YYYY-MM-DD or a timestamp.
    enddateField with each task's end date. A row without one is drawn as a milestone.
    groupcategoryField that colors tasks by team or phase, up to 8 groups.
    progressnumberField with each task's share done, from 0 to 1 (values above 1 are read as percentages). Fills the bar that far and labels it after the bar.

    treemap

    Part-to-whole for many categories: tiles sized by value, kept close to square.

    Share of one whole Nested breakdowns Comparing amounts across categories

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Many parts of one whole: revenue by customer, spend by vendor
    • Portfolios grouped by segment

    Least useful for

    • Two or three parts (use donut)
    • Precise comparisons (use hbar)
    • Negative values

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per category, each named once. How it is built: One tile per row, its area its share of the sum of value, kept close to square; an optional group field clusters tiles. Reads well with 4 to 120 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField naming each tile.
    valuenumberyesField sizing each tile. Zero and negative values are left out.
    groupcategoryField that colors related tiles alike, up to 8 groups. Without it every tile shares one color.

    variance

    Variance against plan, as in financial reporting: per row a bar from a zero line to actual minus plan, right when over and left when under, colored good or bad and labelled with its sign.

    Actual against target or plan What drives or moves a total Comparing amounts across categories

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Budget against actual per line item
    • Financial variance reports where the sign and size of each miss matter

    Least useful for

    • Data with no plan or budget (use hbar)

    The table it needs

    waterfall

    A bridge: how a total moves to another through increases and decreases, each floating from the running total, with totals standing on zero.

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    labelcategoryyesField naming each step.
    valuenumberyesField with each step's change, or the amount for total rows.

    whitespace

    The cross-sell map (whitespace analysis): one cell per client and product, filled where the client holds the product, outlined where it is an opportunity (tinted by how likely), blank where the client is not eligible.

    How each group or period splits Exact values and lookup Comparing amounts across categories

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • Cross-sell and upsell: which clients could take which products, and where to start
    • Product penetration across a book, with the money still on the table
    • A relationship manager's weekly whitespace review

    Least useful for

    • Amounts without a held, open or not eligible state (use heatmap)
    • More than about 16 products or 30 clients at once (filter or group first)
    • One client alone (use xray)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One row per combination of two categories, such as month and product. How it is built: One cell per row and column pair, read from its state: a filled square where held, an outlined square tinted by score where open, a faint dot where not eligible; each row ends with its penetration and the potential still open, each column with how many hold it and how many could; rows sort by potential. Reads well with 4 to 480 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    rowcategoryyesField naming each row, usually the client.
    columncategoryyesField naming each column, usually the product.
    statecategoryyesField saying whether the row holds the column, could (an opportunity), or is not eligible. See states.
    scorenumberField with how likely each opportunity is, 0 to 100 (a propensity). An opportunity cell's tint strengthens with it.
    valuenumberField with the money in each cell: revenue where held, potential where open. Written in the tooltip; the open cells' sum ends each row.

    state Statuscategorystate3 different: Holds, Opportunity, Not eligible

    xray

    A client x-ray: one client on one card, from its first row.

    A headline number Exact values and lookup Profiles across several attributes

    The chart live, the table it needs, its data, and the charts the same data makes

    Best for

    • One client on one card: a pre-meeting brief, a client page, a relationship manager's cockpit
    • Seeing holdings, share of wallet, trend and next steps at one glance

    Least useful for

    • Several clients (use whitespace or table)
    • One number alone (use kpi)
    • A history of events (use history)

    The table it needs

    One row is: One value; with more rows, the last one is the headline and the rest draw its trend. How it is built: The first row's name and detail line, up to six facts as labelled figures, true/false product fields as pills (held in color), a share-of-wallet meter, a list of numbers as a small trend, and lists of flags and next best actions. Reads well with 1 to 1 rows.

    OptionHoldsRequiredWhat it does
    labelcategoryyesField with the client's name.
    detailcategoryField for the line under the name, such as the segment or the relationship manager.
    factsnumber (one or more)Up to six fields shown as small labelled figures: assets, revenue, products held, client since.
    holdingscategory (one or more)True/false fields, one per product, drawn as a strip of named pills: held in color, not held outlined.
    walletnumberField with the share of wallet, 0 to 1, drawn as a meter with its percent.
    trendcategoryField whose value is a list of numbers (revenue by month, say), drawn as a small trend with its first and last values written.
    flagscategoryField whose value is a list of short warnings, shown as quiet amber pills: ["No contact in 90 days", "Fee leakage"].
    actionscategoryField whose value is a list of next best actions, shown as a short checklist.

    • anomalies: It needs readings over time per metric, with a yes/no flag or a low and high band.
    • board: It needs a stage or status column with a handful of values, and a name per row.
    • bullet: It needs a target, plan or budget column.
    • bump: It needs one value per series in each period, to rank.
    • calendar: needs a date column for date
    • candlestick: It needs open, high, low and close prices per period.
    • chord: It needs flows that go both ways between the same groups.
    • choropleth: needs a column of country or state codes that sit on a basemap
    • dual: It needs two measures over the same periods, in two columns.
    • dumbbell: It needs the same measure at two points in time, in two columns.
    • funnel: It needs ordered stages that narrow, such as visits to sign-ups to sales.
    • history: It needs dated events with a short title each.
    • lifecycle: view: stages needs at least two date fields in order, such as ["proposed", "adopted"].
    • likert: It needs answer counts on one ordered scale, such as disagree to agree.
    • locator: needs named places with region codes on a basemap, or coordinates
    • matrix: It needs one row per pair of two categories, such as topic and quarter.
    • meter: It needs a target, plan or budget column.
    • pyramid: It needs two counts per ordered band, such as women and men per age group.
    • ragboard: It needs status columns holding R, A, G (or red, amber, green), one row per client or deal; the rag transform makes them from numbers.
    • ragtrend: It needs one status (R, A, G) per entity per period.
    • rings: It needs a target, plan or budget column.
    • slope: It needs the same measure at two points in time, in two columns.
    • strips: It needs whole counts per row, in one or more part columns.
    • symbols: needs a column of country or state codes that sit on a basemap, or coordinates
    • timeline: needs a date column for start
    • variance: It needs a target, plan or budget column.
    • waterfall: It needs changes that add up from one total to another.
    • whitespace: It needs one row per client and product with a state: held, an opportunity, or not eligible.
